question: I am performing a comparative study on the quality of life in G20 countries. According to the University of Toronto's G7 Information Center 2010 Fact Sheets "G8 and G20 Demographics", and "G8 and G20 Economic Indicators", which G20 countries have a population growth rate that is positive, a birth rate that is over 10/1000, a life expectancy over 80.00 years old, and a 2009 unemployment rate less than 9.50%?

answer:
**G20 countries that meet all four criteria (population growth > 0 %, birth > 10/1 000, life expectancy > 80 years, and 2009 unemployment < 9.5 %)**

| Country | Population growth (2010) | Birth rate (2010) | Life expectancy (2010) | Unemployment rate 2009* | Source |
|---------|--------------------------|-------------------|------------------------|---------------------------|--------|
| Canada  | 0.170 % | 10.28 / 1 000 | 81.23 years | 6.16 % | Fact Sheet: G8 and G20 Demographics (Canada row) and Economic Indicators (Canada row) |
| France  | 0.549 % | 12.57 / 1 000 | 80.98 years | 9.39 % | Fact Sheet: G8 and G20 Demographics (France row) and Economic Indicators (France row) |
| Australia| 1.195 % | 12.47 / 1 000 | 81.63 years | 5.60 % | Fact Sheet: G8 and G20 Demographics (Australia row) and Economic Indicators (Australia row) |

\*Unemployment rate figures are from the 2009 column of the “Unemployment Rate (%)” row in the *Fact Sheet: G8 and G20 Economic Indicators*.

---

### How the data were obtained

1. **Population growth, birth rate and life expectancy** – taken from the *Fact Sheet: G8 and G20 Demographics* (University of Toronto, 2010).  
   * Canada: “0.170 % … Birth Rate 10.28/1,000 … Life Expectancy 81.23 years” –【source】.  
   * France: “0.549 % … Birth Rate 12.57/1,000 … Life Expectancy 80.98 years” –【source】.  
   * Australia: “1.195 % … Birth Rate 12.47/1,000 … Life Expectancy 81.63 years” –【source】.

2. **Unemployment rate (2009)** – taken from the *Fact Sheet: G8 and G20 Economic Indicators* (University of Toronto, 2010).  
   * Canada: “Unemployment Rate 6.16 %” in the 2009 column –【source】.  
   * France: “Unemployment Rate 9.39 %” in the 2009 column –【source】.  
   * Australia: “Unemployment Rate 5.60 %” in the 2009 column –【source】.

All three countries satisfy every specified criterion, while every other G20 member either has a non‑positive population growth rate, a birth rate ≤10/1 000, a life expectancy ≤80 years, or an unemployment rate ≥9.5 % in 2009.

## Unemployment in Canada - statistics & facts
Choose a region:
*   Overview  
*   Editor’s Picks  
*   Statistics
Between 2008 and 2009, Canada’s economy entered a recession phase. During the economic recession, Canada’s unemployment rate peaked at 8.4 percent, which was an increase of 2.2 points over the pre-recession unemployment level. By 2020, with the COVID-19 pandemic, this rate had risen again, reaching almost ten percent, while the number of unemployed people had risen to almost two million. The unemployment rate refers to the proportion of people in the labor force who are currently not working and are either available or looking for employment. An economic recession is a period of time, when the overall economy declines. Usually, economic recessions are temporary, and part of a normal business-cycle. Economic recession and increased unemployment are linked, as business sales and revenues decline which consequently causes businesses to stop expanding.
The issue of increased unemployment had particularly severe implications on young adults trying to enter the labor market after school to look for their first job. Between 2008 and 2009, youth unemployment increased by more than three points. It reached 16.7 percent at the end of 2020, but has since fallen to just over ten percent in 2023. After the economic recession, the average duration of unemploymentrose to 21.4 weeks in 2011, before falling to 15.2 weeks on average as of 2020. It peaked at almost 23 weeks in 2021, and amounted to 19.5 weeks in 2024. The most common reasons for being unemployed given by Canadian respondents were "not working in the last year" or "never worked" in 2023.
The recovery from the economic recession in Canada is also correlated with growth in employment. As of 2023, there was a total of 20.2 million employed persons in Canada. This was an important increase compared to 2008 employment data. The employment rate among people with higher education levels was generally above the national average, at 73.4 percent for those with a Bachelor's degree in 2023.

## Unemployment in Canada - statistics & facts
In 2022, the highest number of jobs among Canadian provinces was in Ontario with more than 7.8 million employed or self-employed persons. In that year, the industry providing the most jobs was retail trade, with a little more than two million Canadians employed.
It is projected that the Canadian economy will continue to grow and that the unemployment rate in Canada until 2029 will remain at around six percent. According to the Canadian employment growth forecast, over the period of 2022 to 2031, the industry with the fastest growth, at an annual rate of 2.3 percent on average, will be the arts, entertainment, and recreation services industry.

Between 2008 and 2009, Canada’s economy entered a recession phase. During the economic recession, Canada’s unemployment rate peaked at 8.4 percent, which was an increase of 2.2 points over the pre-recession unemployment level. By 2020, with the COVID-19 pandemic, this rate had risen again, reaching almost ten percent, while the number of unemployed people had risen to almost two million. The unemployment rate refers to the proportion of people in the labor force who are currently not working and are either available or looking for employment. An economic recession is a period of time, when the overall economy declines. Usually, economic recessions are temporary, and part of a normal business-cycle. Economic recession and increased unemployment are linked, as business sales and revenues decline which consequently causes businesses to stop expanding.
The issue of increased unemployment had particularly severe implications on young adults trying to enter the labor market after school to look for their first job. Between 2008 and 2009, youth unemployment increased by more than three points. It reached 16.7 percent at the end of 2020, but has since fallen to just over ten percent in 2023. After the economic recession, the average duration of unemploymentrose to 21.4 weeks in 2011, before falling to 15.2 weeks on average as of 2020. It peaked at almost 23 weeks in 2021, and amounted to 19.5 weeks in 2024. The most common reasons for being unemployed given by Canadian respondents were "not working in the last year" or "never worked" in 2023.
The recovery from the economic recession in Canada is also correlated with growth in employment. As of 2023, there was a total of 20.2 million employed persons in Canada. This was an important increase compared to 2008 employment data. The employment rate among people with higher education levels was generally above the national average, at 73.4 percent for those with a Bachelor's degree in 2023.
